query: If diarizers do not provide posteriors, which fallback strategies (N-best assignments, weighted sampling, multiple imputation) best preserve speaker-assignment uncertainty?

response.query: If diarizers do not provide posteriors, which fallback strategies (N-best assignments, weighted sampling, multiple imputation) best preserve speaker-assignment uncertainty?
response.answer: N-best assignments and weighted sampling best preserve speaker-assignment uncertainty when diarizers do not provide posteriors. Multiple imputation is also effective but more complex.

results.content: # Quantifying Uncertainty for Data Imputation Methods. # Quantifying Uncertainty for Data Imputation Methods#. Imputation methods comprise a particular approach to deal with missing data. This article presents single and multiple data imputation as methods to complete data sets with missing values. Single imputation methods generate one value for each missing data point. That is why mean imputation is sometimes regarded as “the worst missing data handling method available” [Enders, 2010], p. Fig. 40 shows imputed data for the missing job performances of not hired applicants. As a result, this imputation method yields unbiased and consistent parameter estimates from the filled-in data under an MAR assumption. These methods consist of imputing different values for the resampled incomplete data in order to compute the variability of point estimates of parameters. Besides, it is assumed the original statistical analysis on the completed data set yields estimate(s) \(\hat{\theta}\) of the parameter(s) of interest \(\theta\). Using some single imputation method on every sample \(S^{(b)}\) yields the filled-in samples \(\hat{S}^{(b)},~b=1,\dots,B.\) Then, the parameter estimates \(\hat{\theta}^{(b)},~b=1,\dots,B,\) can be computed for every \(\hat{S}^{(b)}.\) The bootstrap estimate is defined by. The missing values of \(S^{(\setminus i)}\) are filled in with a chosen imputation technique yielding the complete sample \(\hat{S}^{(\setminus i)}.\) The corresponding parameter estimate(s) is (are) denoted by \(\hat{\theta}^{(\setminus i)}.\) For \(\tilde{\theta}\_i=n\hat{\theta}-(n-1)\hat{\theta}^{(\setminus i)}\), the jackknife estimate is then given by. In contrast to single imputation methods, multiple imputation creates several copies of an incomplete data set imputed with different values for each missing data point. Within this phase, it imputes different values for the missing data. The analysis phase consists of performing the actual intended statistical analysis on the \(D\) filled-in data sets from the imputation phase. In this section, we present methods to quantify uncertainty of parameter estimates induced by multiple imputation. The “within-imputation variance” estimates the sampling error that would have resulted if the data had been complete. Due to multiple imputation, we also need to account for the fluctuation of parameter estimates across the \(D\) data sets caused by the different imputed values. where \(\hat{\theta}\_t\), for \(t=1,\dots,D,\) and \(\bar{\theta}\) are again the single parameter estimates from the \(D\) data sets and the multiple imputation point estimate, respectively.

results.title: Using Multiple Imputation Techniques in Data Analysis - Cross Validated
results.content: # Using Multiple Imputation Techniques in Data Analysis. I recently worked with two different statisticians who both suggested different strategies for dealing with imputation of missing data. I've been told by by Statistician A that a multiple imputation technique (like PMM or CART (mice package in R)) is the most robust method to use. And I understand that you cannot "pool" the data outside of a statistical test by averaging or stacking the data to combine all imputed datasets into a single dataset. However, if one wants to use a multiple imputation to generate a complete (single) dataset for data visualization purposes (ex. Statistician B always goes by the book and stated that data imputed via multiple imputation can only be used in analyses where the results can be pooled (linear regression). This stance is also confusing given the large number of published papers that mention the use of multiple imputation and do not ever describe pooling results or changing the method when producing visualizations, etc. And in a case where I do need to use a regression technique and I employ multiple imputation, but then would like to visualize the results, do I create a visualization with each imputed dataset or choose the values from just one? The value of multiple imputation is that, when pooling results across imputed datasets, the uncertainty in the imputed values (which are not known but estimated) is properly captured. For an inferential statistic like a regression coefficient, this is the reason you can't simply 'pool' the data by averaging across imputations before fitting the model. So in this case why not just 'pool' your data by averaging across imputations? I kind of lean towards Statistician B: If the results can be pooled across imputed datasets (e.g., regression coefficient, mean/median), I would use multiple imputation; if the purpose is to visualise, for example, the changes/patterns of some variables in a single dataset, I wouldn't use multiple imputation. 0") Multiple data imputation to use in model. 2") Compare the output of a pooled model after multiple imputation vs model on combined long dataset. 2") Creating a Pooled Data Set From Multiple Imputation Output in SPSS.
